sentences: Last night, after a tough day at work, I sat down on the couch with a sigh.
My dog, who was playing in the garden, immediately came over and rested his head on my knees.
Coincidence?
Habit?
Or did he really 'understand' me?
This question is one that all pet owners ask themselves.
And for about twenty years, science has been taking it seriously.
Let's start with the dog, the most studied animal.
The results are impressive.
An average dog can learn to recognize several dozen words; some exceptional dogs, trained by researchers, can distinguish several hundred.
But vocabulary is just the visible part.
The real talent of the dog lies elsewhere: it reads our emotions.
Experiments have shown that dogs can tell the difference between a happy human face and an angry one, even in simple photos.
They are also sensitive to the tone of voice: the same words, spoken cheerfully or harshly, do not elicit the same reaction at all.
This talent is no coincidence.
Dogs have been living with us for tens of thousands of years.
During all this time, the dogs that understood humans best were the best fed and protected.
Generation after generation, evolution has created a specialist of the human species.
And what about the cat?
Its case is more amusing.
For a long time, people believed it understood nothing — or didn't want to understand anything.
Recent studies tell a different story.
The cat perfectly recognizes its name: Japanese researchers demonstrated this by observing the ears and heads of cats listening to different words.
The cat also distinguishes its owner's voice from that of a stranger.
Simply put, it doesn't always see the point in responding.
Understanding and obeying are two different things — and the cat has chosen its side.
However, we must be honest about the limits.
Our animals do not understand our sentences the way we do.
When I tell my dog, 'we're going to the park after lunch,' he catches 'park' and the rest gets lost.
Grammar, abstract ideas, the past, and the future remain beyond their reach, as far as we know.
But is that so important?
My dog doesn't understand my sentences; he understands my sighs, my silences, my joy, and my fatigue.
Communication doesn't always happen through words.
Last night, on the couch, the question didn't even arise.
He understood perfectly.

sentences: Stress is a part of modern life.
Work, money, family, world news: there are plenty of reasons to feel under pressure.
A little stress is normal, and even useful.
But too much stress, for too long, wears out the body and mind.
When we are stressed, the body reacts: the heart beats faster, the muscles tense up, and we sleep poorly.
We become irritable and have less energy.
If this state lasts, it can harm our health.
It is therefore important to learn to manage stress.
The first thing to do is simple: breathe.
When we feel overwhelmed, a few slow, deep breaths already calm the body.
Closing our eyes, inhaling gently, exhaling slowly: it costs nothing and really helps.
We also need to know how to take breaks.
We often believe that we have to work without stopping to be effective.
That's false.
A short break to walk, drink tea, or look out the window allows the mind to relax and unwind.
Finally, stress and sleep are linked.
A tired person handles pressure less well.
Protecting our nights is also about protecting our calm.
We cannot eliminate all the stress from our lives.
But we can learn to live better with it by listening to our bodies and giving ourselves a few real moments of calm each day.

sentences: We use energy at every moment, almost without thinking about it: to light our homes, to heat ourselves, to move around, and to power our devices.
All it takes is to press a button.
But behind this ordinary action lies an essential, and rarely asked, question: where does this energy actually come from?
Because not all sources are equal, far from it.
For two centuries, most of our energy has come from fossil fuels: coal, oil, and gas.
They have a huge advantage — they are powerful and easy to use — but a major drawback: burning them releases enormous gas emissions, which are the main contributors to global warming.
Moreover, these resources are not infinite; one day, they will run out.
In the face of this dual problem, renewable energies are developing.
As their name suggests, they do not run out: solar energy captures sunlight, wind energy uses the wind, and others harness the water from rivers.
Their great merit is that they produce energy with almost no pollution.
Their limitations are real too: the sun does not shine at night, the wind does not always blow, and we must therefore learn to store this energy and balance the grid.
The transition from one model to another is one of the greatest challenges of our time.
It is complicated, costly, and no one claims it will be easy.
Changing the way an entire country produces its energy does not happen in just a few years.
This question goes far beyond our individual actions: turning off a light is a good habit, but the key decisions are made at the level of countries and companies, in the choices they make today.
However, understanding where our energy comes from is not useless.
An informed citizen makes better choices, supports better decisions, and stops believing that electricity comes, as if by magic, from the wall socket.
Behind every switch, there is a societal choice.

sentences: Last month, I had a fight with Léa, my best friend.
It was our first real argument in six years.
It all started over a small thing.
We were supposed to plan a weekend together.
I had everything prepared.
Three days before, Léa told me that she could no longer come.
I was disappointed.
What hurt me was the reason: she had accepted an invitation to a party.
I told her this on the phone, and I spoke too loudly.
She replied that I always decided everything without asking her opinion.
We both hung up angry.
Then, there were three weeks of silence.
Every day, I thought about writing to her, but I didn't do it.
I was waiting for her to start.
I believe she was doing the same thing.
Finally, one Sunday evening, I sent her a simple message: 'I miss you.
Can we see each other?'
She replied in ten minutes: 'Yes.
I also wanted to write to you.'
We met on Tuesday and talked for three hours.
She was right about one thing: I organize too much without asking.
And I was right too.
We learned that we shouldn't let three weeks go by.
In January, we went to spend a day at the sea.
Many people find this idea strange: the sea is for summer.
We arrived around eleven o'clock.
It was six degrees and there was a lot of wind.
The beach was completely empty.
In August, there are thousands of people here, and you have to arrive by nine o'clock to find a spot.
That day, we saw four people in three hours: an elderly couple, a man with a dog, and a fisherman.
The town was different too.
Half of the restaurants and shops were closed until April, with signs on the doors: 'Reopening on April 1st.'
We walked on the beach for an hour.
The wind was strong and cold; you had to speak loudly to hear each other.
My children collected seashells and ran in front of the waves.
The sea was gray and rough, with high, noisy waves.
It wasn't the sea from postcards.
It was wilder, and I found it more beautiful.
At noon, we found the only open restaurant, with only locals inside.
The owner told us: 'You are right to come now.'
In winter, the sea is ours.

sentences: It is often forgotten that French only became the majority language in France relatively late.
At the time of the Revolution, a significant part of the population spoke another language first: Breton, Occitan, Basque, Alsatian, Corsican, Flemish, Catalan, and many variants.
The decline of these languages was not spontaneous.
It resulted from a deliberate policy, implemented from the nineteenth century, based on the idea that national unity required a single language.
Schools played a central role.
Many accounts report punishments given to students caught speaking their mother tongue in the schoolyard.
This policy produced a lasting effect, less through prohibition than through shame: many parents stopped passing their language on to their children, convinced that it would disadvantage them.
It is this mechanism — the halt of family transmission — that causes a language to disappear, much more surely than regulations.
Since the 1970s, a counter-movement has begun.
Associative and bilingual schools have emerged, the law has evolved, and these languages are now recognized as part of France's heritage.
The results are mixed.
The number of speakers continues to decline, as the generations who spoke these languages daily are disappearing.
But the number of students enrolled in Breton or Occitan is increasing.
These new speakers do not speak exactly the same language as their grandparents.
A language learned at school is never identical to an inherited language.
However, it has a decisive advantage: it is still here.

sentences: The relationship between France and the United Kingdom is long-standing, marked by conflicts, alliances, and a long tradition of mutual teasing.
What is more interesting are the discreet admirations.
What many Britons envy about France is its healthcare system, often praised for its accessibility and waiting times.
The quality of everyday food, especially the fact that a decent meal remains affordable.
The importance given to leisure time.
And a land use planning that has maintained public services in medium-sized towns, while British centralization in London has been more brutal.
What many French people envy about the UK is a lighter and faster administration.
A labor market where it is easier to bounce back after a failure, including after bankruptcy.
A culture of customer service often considered friendlier.
And a more relaxed attitude towards hierarchy and qualifications — in France, the school attended at twenty still matters at fifty.
There are also mutual criticisms, equally revealing.
The French find the British indirect, to the point that you never really know what they think.
The British find the French abrupt, even aggressive, while it is often just a straightforwardness they embrace.
These misunderstandings have a common point: each interprets the other through their own codes.
Tom sums things up in his own way.
"In England, we say 'it's interesting' when we think it's bad.
In France, we say it's bad."
"It shocked me for two years."
"Now, it saves me time."

sentences: Making bread seems simple: flour, water, salt, yeast.
However, between these ingredients and a nice loaf, a remarkable biological phenomenon occurs.
Yeast is a living organism: a microscopic fungus.
When it is mixed into a dough, it finds food in the sugars of the flour.
By consuming them, it produces gas — carbon dioxide — as well as small amounts of alcohol.
It is this gas that makes the dough rise.
Trapped in the network formed by the proteins of the flour — gluten — it inflates the mass like thousands of tiny bubbles.
Without gluten, the gas would escape and the bread would remain flat, which explains why gluten-free breads are harder to make rise.
Time and temperature play a crucial role.
In warmth, the yeast works quickly; in cold, slowly.
That’s why many bakers let their dough rest in the refrigerator overnight: slow fermentation develops more flavors.
During baking, the heat causes a final push of the gas, then sets the structure and kills the yeast.
The alcohol, on the other hand, evaporates.
Sourdough, older than baker's yeast, is based on the same principle, but with a natural mix of microorganisms captured from the air and the flour.
It gives a more sour taste and better preservation.
Understanding this changes the way we cook.
We stop following a recipe blindly.
We start working with a living organism, which has its own preferences and pace.

sentences: In front of a landscape, a monument, or a scene that moves us, our first gesture is almost always the same: we take out a camera and we photograph.
This reflex, which has become universal, seems innocent, even useful — isn't it about keeping a record of what we experience?
However, a question deserves to be asked: by constantly photographing what we see, do we still really see it?
Disturbing research suggests that photographing a scene can, paradoxically, harm the memory we have of it.
When we entrust the camera with the task of retaining, our attention relaxes, as if we are offloading the effort of memorizing onto it.
We then look less intensely, confident that the image will preserve for us what we haven't really taken the time to contemplate.
Photography, which is supposed to fix memories, risks impoverishing them instead.
There's more.
The act of photographing interposes a screen between us and what we are experiencing.
Preoccupied with framing, adjusting, and capturing the right angle, we cease to be fully present at the scene; we treat it as an image to capture rather than a moment to live.
The direct, immediate experience fades behind its reproduction.
We bring back thousands of snapshots, and sometimes very few genuinely felt memories.
This phenomenon worsens when photography is no longer intended for us, but for others.
Photographing to show, to publish, to prove that we were there transforms the experience into a spectacle.
We no longer look at a place for itself, but for the image we will take from it; we choose what we see based on what will 'look good'.
The elsewhere becomes a backdrop, and the journey, a collection of images intended for the gaze of others.
Should we then give up photographing?
That would be excessive, as the image also has its virtues: it can revive a memory, prolong an emotion, share a beauty.
The problem is not photography itself, but its automatism, which makes us capture before we have looked.
We can photograph differently: less, better, after having first contemplated.
Perhaps we should, in front of what moves us, resist the first reflex and start by looking — really, for a long time, without a camera.
Then, only afterwards, decide if we want to keep an image of it.
For no photograph will ever replace what we haven't taken the time to see.

sentences: What makes a multitude of individuals, often very different, feel like members of the same nation?
Neither just territory, nor just language, nor just laws are enough to explain this.
What unites a people is also, and perhaps above all, a narrative: a common story they tell about their origins, their trials, their glories, and their purpose.
Nations hold together through these shared narratives as much as through their borders.
This national narrative serves a real and valuable function.
It creates a sense of belonging, connects strangers in an imagined community, and gives individuals the feeling of participating in something that transcends and precedes them.
Without this narrative link, a nation would be nothing more than a juxtaposition of individuals with nothing in common.
Foundational narratives, celebrated heroes, and commemorated great moments weave this invisible solidarity without which no lasting communal life is possible.
But these narratives have an inherent flaw: they simplify, embellish, and sometimes distort.
To unite, a national narrative tends to smooth over rough edges, magnify glories, and silence shames, presenting as a natural truth what was the product of chance and violence.
It transforms a complex and often troubled history into a coherent and flattering narrative.
In doing so, it strays from the truth and can become a myth that blinds more than it enlightens.
The danger arises when this narrative, instead of simply uniting, begins to exclude and oppose.
For a national narrative can also be constructed against others: by designating enemies, glorifying its own superiority, and fostering contempt or hatred for those who are not part of it.
History shows the disasters that can result from perverted national narratives, when a people tells itself a story of greatness and purity that justifies aggression or exclusion.
The narrative that unites can also arm.
Should we then renounce all national narratives in the name of historical truth alone?
That would be both impossible and dangerous.
Impossible, because no community can do without a narrative; dangerous, because the void left would quickly be filled by cruder narratives.
The issue is not to eliminate the narrative, but to demand it be more honest: capable of uniting without lying, of founding a belonging without denying complexity, of being proud without being blind.
An adult nation is one that can tell itself a true story, with its glories and its faults, and still find a way to hold together.
This is a difficult balance, always threatened, between the myth that unites and the truth that liberates.
But it is under this condition that a common narrative can gather the living without arming them against others.

sentences: We spontaneously associate communication with speech: to communicate means to speak, to say, to express oneself with words.
In this perspective, silence is merely an absence, a void, the interruption of true communication.
However, this conception is incomplete.
For silence is not just the absence of words; it is itself full of meaning, it communicates in its own way, and it plays a role in our exchanges that chatter often makes us forget.
Silence, first of all, speaks.
A silence after a question can express embarrassment, disagreement, contemplation, or refusal.
A silence shared between two close individuals conveys an understanding that no words could express better.
A silence in the face of another's suffering can be worth more than all verbal consolations.
Silence is not a gap in communication; it is a modality of it, as rich and sometimes more accurate than speech.
What we leave unsaid means as much as what we say.
Silence also has its own value, which our era tends to ignore.
We live in a world saturated with words, noise, and demands, where silence has become rare and almost suspicious.
We rush to fill it, as if it were unbearable, filling every void with music, words, and content.
Yet this silence that we flee is precisely what the mind needs to settle, reflect, and feel.
It is often in silence that the deepest thoughts are born, where the inner life unfolds that constant noise stifles.
In the very act of exchange, silence has virtues that abundant speech cannot replace.
Knowing how to be silent to truly listen, allowing the other person space to express themselves, and not filling every pause with words: this is a form of attention and respect.
Those who speak incessantly do not listen; they occupy the space, preventing the other from existing.
Silence, on the contrary, makes room for the other, and this space is the foundation of any true encounter.
There is an eloquence in attentive silence that no discourse can match.
Of course, it is not about making silence an absolute value, nor about despising speech, which remains the best means of understanding and connecting with one another.
Silence also has its shadows: it can be an escape, cowardice, or a refusal to say what should be said.
Being silent when one should speak, keeping silence in the face of injustice, is not a virtue.
Silence does not hold value in itself; it is valued for what it carries and for the moment when we choose it.
Thus, silence indeed has meaning, and even several.
Far from being the simple opposite of communication, it is an essential part of it, which our talkative culture has unlearned to hear.

Rediscovering the meaning of silence — knowing how to be silent, listen, leave space, and inhabit the voids rather than flee from them — may be a way to regain a part of what the overflow of words has made us lose.

sentences: Few countries know each other as well while understanding each other so poorly as France and Great Britain.

Separated by a stretch of sea that can be crossed in a few hours, linked by a thousand years of shared history, wars, alliances, and exchanges, the two neighbors maintain a unique relationship, characterized by attraction and rivalry, fascination and mutual mockery.
Observing them together helps us understand how two such close nations could forge such different characters.
History, first and foremost, has intertwined them intimately.

There was a time when the kings of England spoke French, when the two crowns disputed the same lands, and when their destinies were so intertwined that it was not always clear how to distinguish them.
From this ancient proximity emerged a singular blend: the English language itself is filled with words from French, remnants of this shared history.
The two peoples are not strangers to each other; rather, they are old relatives who know each other too well.
And yet, what differences there are.
Where the French love principles, general ideas, and grand abstract debates, the British are wary of theories and prefer pragmatism, specific cases, and solutions that work.
Where France made its revolution and broke with its past, Great Britain preferred slow evolution, maintaining its monarchy and traditions while transforming.
These two temperaments — one more inclined towards logic and rupture, the other towards compromise and continuity — are reflected in countless aspects of life in both countries.
These differences fuel stereotypes that each side delights in maintaining.
The French readily see the British as distant, obsessed with politeness and the weather, and poor eaters; the British see the French as arrogant, undisciplined, quick to strike, and moralizers.
These caricatures, like all caricatures, distort while capturing something.
They primarily express the pleasure these two neighbors take in defining themselves against each other, each needing the other as a foil and a mirror.
For beneath the mockery often lies a secret fascination.
The French sometimes dream of British phlegm, that ability to remain calm, and that humor which diffuses everything.
The British sometimes envy the French art of living, their appreciation for good food, conversation, and pleasure without guilt.
Each finds in the other what they lack, and perhaps that is why, despite the jibes, the two peoples never tire of each other.
Understanding the relationship between France and Great Britain is therefore grasping much more than a neighborhood rivalry.
It is observing how two nations, stemming from a shared history, have taken opposite paths, and how they continue, even today, to define themselves in relation to one another.

These articles will explore some of these differences — in relation to the state, food, rules, and daily life — not to determine who is right, but to understand what each reveals about the other and about ourselves.

sentences: Our societies operate twenty-four hours a day, which means that every night, millions of people work while others sleep.
This night work, once reserved for a few professions, has expanded as life has sped up and the demand for constant availability has gained ground.
However, this night work, which we all benefit from, has a cost that is often underestimated, and it weighs heavily on those who perform it.
The first cost is physiological, and it is significant.
Our bodies are set to a day-night rhythm deeply ingrained in our biology: we are made to be active during the day and sleep at night.
Working at night and sleeping during the day goes against this internal clock, and the body pays the price.
Daytime sleep is shorter and less restorative; fatigue accumulates; and research links prolonged night work to various health issues.
Those who stay awake for us wear out their bodies in ways we do not see.
The second cost is social.
Living on a different schedule means living partly out of sync with others.
The night worker sleeps when their loved ones are awake, works when they are resting, and struggles to share meals, evenings, and moments of communal life.
Their family and social life suffers, out of tune with that of their surroundings.
They inhabit a parallel world, awake when their loved ones sleep, and this desynchronization is a form of solitude, all the more harsh because it is invisible.
What is striking is that this difficult and costly work is often done by the most modest.
Night jobs — cleaning, security, caregiving, handling, service — are among the least well-paid and least recognized.
Those who pay the highest physical and social price are rarely the ones who reap the greatest benefits.
There is a subtle injustice here: the hardship of the night often adds to the precariousness of the day, hitting the same people twice.
Recognizing this does not lead to calling for an end to all night work, part of which is essential: we will not close hospitals at night.
But it does invite us to distinguish between necessary night work and that which is not, imposed solely by the relentless pursuit of constant availability and profitability.
Some of our nighttime activity is less about a real need than about an immediate consumption demand that we could forgo without much harm.
It especially calls for better recognition, protection, and compensation for those who work at night to keep the city running.
The minimum would be not to forget their existence, to acknowledge what we owe them, and to compensate for the hardship they endure on our behalf.
For the comfort of our days relies, in part, on the sacrifice of their nights — and it would at least be fair not to ignore that.

sentences: Our societies have a genuine cult of youth.
Youth is presented everywhere as the ideal: we want to appear young, stay young, and we dread aging as if it were a decline.
In this context, old age has become something we hide, push away, and talk about with embarrassment.
This devaluation of age, so contrary to what other eras and cultures have known, deserves to be questioned, as it may deprive us of something important.
It hasn't always been this way, and it isn't this way everywhere.
Many societies have given elderly people a prominent place, seeing them as bearers of wisdom, memory, and experience.
Old age was respected, listened to, and honored there; aging meant gaining authority and consideration.
It's no coincidence that so many traditions have made the old person a figure of wisdom: age, it was said, brings knowledge that youth cannot have, that which comes from having lived a long time.
Our era has largely broken with this vision.
Several reasons have contributed to this.
The pace of change, first: in a world that transforms so quickly, the experience of the elders seems quickly outdated, their knowledge obsolete, so that old age appears to have lost its usefulness.
The cult of performance and productivity, next, which values vigor and efficiency, and relegates those who no longer produce.
A society focused on the future, novelty, and speed struggles to make room for those who embody duration and slowness.
However, this relegation has a cost, for the elderly as well as for society as a whole.
For the elderly, it means exclusion, uselessness, and loneliness; they are pushed out of active life, confined to separate places, and no longer listened to.
For society, it represents a loss: that of everything elderly people could transmit — experience, memory, perspective, a different relationship with time.
By relegating its elderly, a society deprives itself of their contribution and condemns itself to endlessly relearn what they could have taught it.
It's not about returning to a naive veneration of age, nor claiming that old age automatically brings wisdom — aging does not necessarily make one wise.
But it is about rejecting the opposite relegation, which sees in old age nothing but a worthless decline.
Between the cult of the old and the cult of youth, there is room for a fair recognition: one that grants each age its own dignity and contribution, without a contemptuous hierarchy.
Giving a place back to the elderly is therefore not only a matter of justice towards them; it is also a way for society not to impoverish itself.
A civilization that only has eyes for youth would be like a being without memory, cut off from its own duration.

Making room for old age, listening to it, honoring it, is to recognize that life is not only valuable for its vigor, and that there is, in having lived a long time, something that deserves respect and attention.

sentences: Having a real discussion with someone who thinks differently has become rare and difficult.
We are increasingly surrounded by people who share our views, in circles where our opinions are reinforced rather than challenged.
And when we encounter contradiction, the exchange often ends abruptly: we become defensive, we insult each other, and everyone leaves more convinced than before.
However, this inability to discuss with our opponents is a impoverishment, and even a danger, that is worth understanding the causes of.
Why do these discussions fail so often?
First, because we generally do not seek to understand, but to win.
We approach disagreement as a battle where the goal is to prevail, not as an opportunity to learn.
As a result, we do not really listen to the other person: we wait for them to stop talking so we can make our argument, we look for their flaws, we caricature their position to better refute it.
A discussion conducted this way can only fail, because neither listens to the other; each speaks for their side, not to their interlocutor.
Next, these exchanges fail because we attribute the worst intentions to our opponents.
We readily assume that someone who thinks differently is acting in bad faith, misinformed, or driven by unacknowledged motives.
This presumption prevents any real discussion: how can you exchange ideas with someone you immediately consider dishonest or stupid?
However, most of the time, our opponent sincerely believes what they say, for reasons that seem valid to them, just like us.
Attributing bad faith to them means avoiding understanding them, and making the exchange impossible.
What would it take for these discussions to become possible again?
First, approach the other person with the assumption of their good faith: assume they have valid reasons for thinking what they think, and seek to understand them before judging.
Next, really listen, not to reply, but to grasp what the other person means, even if it means asking them to clarify.
Finally, accept the idea that we might have something to learn, that the other person could be right on certain points — a mindset without which there is no dialogue, only two monologues.
This does not mean that we must accept everything, abandon our convictions, or treat all opinions as equally valid.
One can listen respectfully to a position and judge it to be false; understand someone's reasons and calmly show them why we believe they are mistaken.
Discussing with an opponent is not giving in; it is seeking together, with respect, what might be true.
One can leave such a discussion without having changed their mind, but having better understood the other person, and sometimes themselves.
The stakes go beyond the comfort of more civil conversations.
A democracy, a society, can only survive if those who think differently can still talk to each other.
When discussion becomes impossible, all that remains is the confrontation of factions, hatred, and sometimes violence.

Relearning to discuss with those who think differently — to listen to them, to attribute them good faith, to accept the possibility of being wrong — is therefore not just a matter of politeness; it is a condition for communal life.
And it starts with a modest but difficult renunciation: that of wanting to always have the last word.

sentences: The past is never neutral in the present; it is a stake, and often a weapon.
Those in power, nations, and movements know this, as they continually mobilize it for their own benefit: to legitimize themselves, to unite a community, to identify enemies, to justify a policy.

This political use of the past, as old as power itself, deserves to be analyzed, because it often operates without our awareness, and readily confuses its ends with those of historical knowledge, which it claims while betraying.
The most common use of the past is legitimization.
A power, a regime, a nation seeks in history the titles of its existence: a glorious origin, continuity, a mission.

One establishes a narrative of origins that grounds the present, celebrates ancestors, commemorates great deeds, and places the current order within a history that seems to make it necessary and just.
This narrative is not necessarily false, but it is always selective: it retains what legitimizes and silences what disturbs, transforming a complex and often violent history into a flattering tale.
The past serves less to understand than to justify.
Another complementary use is the construction of collective identity.
For a group of individuals to feel like a community, there must be a common past, whether real or reconstructed: shared trials, glories, sufferings, heroes.
This common past creates a sense of belonging, the 'we' without which there is no community.
However, in doing so, it also creates a closure: the 'we' is defined against an 'others', and the narrative that unites some can exclude or stigmatize others.
The past mobilized to unite can thus become an instrument of division, designating hereditary enemies, rekindling grudges, justifying hatreds in the name of old wounds.
The most perverse use, finally, is the instrumentalization in service of a present cause.
The past is summoned not to enlighten, but to settle a current debate: such a historical analogy disqualifies an opponent, such a memory justifies a claim, such a precedent legitimizes an action.
The past becomes an arsenal from which everyone draws the weapons for their current battles, even if it means distorting it, simplifying it, or using it anachronistically.
Serious history, which places facts in their context and resists simplifications, then hinders this militant use, which prefers a mythified past, reduced to a few striking and manipulable images.
These uses pose a formidable problem, as they claim to be based on history while betraying it.
They invoke the past, facts, memory, but bend them to ends that are not those of knowledge.
The power that instrumentalizes history does not say that it distorts it; it claims, on the contrary, to restore the truth that others would have obscured.

Distinguishing history from its instrumentalization then becomes difficult, especially since the boundary is not always clear, and the historian themselves is not exempt from the concerns of their time.
But this difficulty should not lead to surrender: between critical work, subject to facts and method, and militant use, subject to a cause, the difference remains, and it is decisive.
In the face of the political uses of the past, the best protection is historical knowledge itself, with its demands for rigor, context, and complexity.

An informed people about its real history, in its greatness and shadows, is better able to resist the myths that others would sell them; an ignorant people, or one that knows only a flattering narrative, is at the mercy of those who manipulate the past.
That is why teaching a critical history, which teaches how to distinguish facts from their use, is not a luxury, but a democratic necessity.
For he who controls the narrative of the past shapes the present — and nothing is more dangerous than a people who knows only what they have been led to believe about their history.

sentences: When faced with a possible but uncertain risk — a product that could be harmful, a technology with poorly understood effects, a threat whose magnitude is not established — should we wait for scientific certainty before acting, or take measures as soon as the danger seems plausible, even without proof?
This question, known as the "precautionary principle," is one of the most delicate of our time, as it engages our relationship with uncertainty, risk, and action.
And the definitive answers, whether one way or the other, also prove to be insufficient.
The precautionary principle, in its common formulation, encourages action in the face of a serious risk even in the absence of scientific certainty about its reality.
Its intuition is powerful: waiting for certain proof of a danger can mean waiting until it’s too late, until the harm is done and irreversible.
Some damages — ecological, health-related — are such that we cannot afford to suffer them just to confirm that they were possible.
In these cases, demanding certainty before acting amounts to betting on the absence of danger, a gamble whose consequences, in the event of an error, would be catastrophic and irreversible.
This caution has its legitimacy, and history supports it in many cases where action was delayed too long, waiting for definitive proof while the harm took hold.

In the face of serious and potentially irreversible risks, the demand for absolute certainty can be a form of irrationality disguised as rigor: it favors inaction, which is not neutral, as it allows the risk to materialize.
Acting in doubt, when the stakes are high, can be wiser than waiting for certainty that will come too late.
But the precautionary principle, taken to the extreme, turns into its opposite and becomes unreasonable.
For every action, every innovation, every product carries possible risks that can never be entirely excluded.

If we were to demand proof of the total absence of danger before allowing anything, we would do nothing: no technology, no medication, no progress would ever come to light, as none can guarantee the absolute absence of risk.

An absolute precautionary principle would paralyze all action, and this paralysis has its own cost: the benefits we forgo, the lives we do not save, the progress we prevent, are also damages, albeit invisible.
There is more.
The inaction promoted by excessive precaution is not without risk; it has its own dangers, often overlooked.
Rejecting a technology out of precaution also means depriving ourselves of its benefits and facing the risks it would have avoided.
The precaution that focuses on the risks of action, while forgetting the risks of inaction, is not true prudence: it is a bias that treats as neutral what is not.
Doing nothing is also a decision, which also entails responsibility.

Wisdom in this matter, therefore, lies neither in refusing to act without certainty nor in demanding certainty before acting, but in a nuanced evaluation: weighing the severity and probability of the risk, its reversibility or not, the costs of action as well as those of inaction, the expected benefits as well as the possible dangers.

In the face of a serious, irreversible, and plausible risk, precaution is necessary; in the face of a minor, uncertain, and reversible risk, demanding action in doubt would paralyze us without reason.
The precautionary principle is a good guide only when tempered by proportion: applied mechanically, in either direction, it leads either to recklessness or paralysis.
Deciding in uncertainty is a difficult art that cannot be reduced to any formula — and claiming that a simple rule could exempt us from it is the illusion that must first be set aside.

sentences: Never has the world been so accessible.
Without leaving our place, we can see the most distant places, attend various events, access a vast amount of human knowledge, and connect with people on the other side of the earth.
The whole world seems to be at our fingertips, available with a gesture.
This unprecedented accessibility is an extraordinary achievement, and it would be ungrateful to underestimate it.
But it raises a question: accessing an image of the world, its representation on a screen, is it really knowing the world, experiencing it, meeting it?
We must first recognize all that this accessibility brings in reality.
Through it, knowledge that was once reserved has opened up to everyone; distant realities have become visible; separated people can connect.
Someone who once only knew their village can now embrace the world with their gaze.
It is a vast opening that has broadened everyone's horizons, broken many isolations, and made available what was previously out of reach.
To disdain this accessibility in the name of an 'authentic' experience reserved for a few privileged individuals would be a contemptible stance.
And yet, access to the representation of something is not the experience of the thing itself, and confusing the two would impoverish oneself unknowingly.
Seeing an image of a place is not the same as being there; knowing its representation is not the same as experiencing it.
Real experience engages our whole being — the body, the senses, presence, lived time — in a way that representation on a screen cannot replicate.

Standing truly in front of a mountain, in a place, beside a person, mobilizes a fullness of perception, a presence, a relationship that the image, however faithful, reduces to its only visual dimension.
The screen shows us, but it does not allow us to live.
This difference is not trivial, as it touches on the very nature of knowledge and experience.
Knowing the world through its representations means knowing it from a distance, from the outside, without the contact that alone allows us to feel.
It risks making us believe we know what we have only seen in an image, confusing information about something with the experience of that thing, mistaking the map for the territory.
However, there are dimensions of reality that can only be revealed through presence, engagement, direct experience — and which remain inaccessible to those who only know the representation.
The world at our fingertips is a world reduced to what can pass through a screen, that is to say, amputated of everything that the screen does not convey.
There is an additional, more insidious risk: that easy access to representation diverts us from real experience, giving us the illusion of it.
Why move, engage, or experience when we can see everything effortlessly on a screen?
This ease can lead to a form of passivity, where we are content to contemplate images of the world instead of living it, where mediated experience replaces direct experience.
We then risk living vicariously, spectators of a world we watch without being in it, knowing everything in image and nothing in reality.
Accessibility, by making real experience seem less necessary, could divert us from it.
It is not about opposing noble real experience to contemptible representation, nor about renouncing the accessibility that has brought so much.
It is about not confusing one with the other, maintaining awareness that seeing is not living, that the image of the world is not the world.

It is to preserve, alongside easy access to representations, the taste and practice of real experience, presence, and direct engagement; it is to remember that certain things can only be known by living them, and that the screen, however valuable for providing access, does not replace this contact with reality of which it only transmits the appearance.
The world at our fingertips is a gift; taking it for the world itself would be to confine ourselves to its representation.

alignments.english: It is a vast opening that has broadened everyone's horizons, broken many isolations, and made available what was previously out of reach.

alignments.french: Mépriser cette accessibilité au nom d'une expérience « authentique » réservée à quelques privilégiés serait une pose méprisable.
alignments.english: To disdain this accessibility in the name of an 'authentic' experience reserved for a few privileged individuals would be a contemptible stance.

alignments.french: Et pourtant, l'accès à la représentation d'une chose n'est pas l'expérience de la chose même, et confondre les deux serait s'appauvrir sans le savoir.
alignments.english: And yet, access to the representation of something is not the experience of the thing itself, and confusing the two would impoverish oneself unknowingly.

alignments.french: Voir l'image d'un lieu n'est pas y être ; en connaître la représentation n'est pas en faire l'expérience.
alignments.english: Seeing an image of a place is not the same as being there; knowing its representation is not the same as experiencing it.

alignments.french: L'expérience réelle engage tout notre être — le corps, les sens, la présence, le temps vécu — d'une manière que la représentation sur un écran ne saurait reproduire.
alignments.english: Real experience engages our whole being — the body, the senses, presence, lived time — in a way that representation on a screen cannot replicate.

alignments.french: Se tenir réellement devant une montagne, dans un lieu, auprès d'une personne, mobilise une plénitude de perception, une présence, un rapport que l'image, si fidèle soit-elle, réduit à sa seule dimension visuelle.
alignments.english: Standing truly in front of a mountain, in a place, beside a person, mobilizes a fullness of perception, a presence, a relationship that the image, however faithful, reduces to its only visual dimension.

alignments.french: L'écran donne à voir, mais il ne donne pas à vivre.
alignments.english: The screen shows us, but it does not allow us to live.

alignments.french: Cette différence n'est pas mince, car elle touche à la nature même de la connaissance et de l'expérience.
alignments.english: This difference is not trivial, as it touches on the very nature of knowledge and experience.

alignments.french: Connaître le monde par ses représentations, c'est le connaître à distance, de l'extérieur, sans le contact qui seul fait éprouver.
alignments.english: Knowing the world through its representations means knowing it from a distance, from the outside, without the contact that alone allows us to feel.

alignments.french: C'est risquer de croire connaître ce qu'on n'a fait que voir en image, de confondre l'information sur une chose avec l'expérience de cette chose, de prendre la carte pour le territoire.
alignments.english: It risks making us believe we know what we have only seen in an image, confusing information about something with the experience of that thing, mistaking the map for the territory.

alignments.french: Or il y a des dimensions du réel qui ne se livrent qu'à la présence, à l'engagement, à l'épreuve directe — et qui restent inaccessibles à qui n'en connaît que la représentation.
alignments.english: However, there are dimensions of reality that can only be revealed through presence, engagement, direct experience — and which remain inaccessible to those who only know the representation.

alignments.french: Le monde à portée d'écran est un monde réduit à ce qui peut passer par un écran, c'est-à-dire amputé de tout ce que l'écran ne transmet pas.
alignments.english: The world at our fingertips is a world reduced to what can pass through a screen, that is to say, amputated of everything that the screen does not convey.

alignments.french: Il y a un risque supplémentaire, plus insidieux : que l'accès facile à la représentation nous détourne de l'expérience réelle, en nous en donnant l'illusion.
alignments.english: There is an additional, more insidious risk: that easy access to representation diverts us from real experience, giving us the illusion of it.

alignments.french: Pourquoi se déplacer, s'engager, éprouver, quand on peut tout voir sans effort sur un écran ?
alignments.english: Why move, engage, or experience when we can see everything effortlessly on a screen?

alignments.french: Cette facilité peut engendrer une forme de passivité, où l'on se contente de contempler des images du monde au lieu de le vivre, où l'expérience médiate remplace l'expérience directe.
alignments.english: This ease can lead to a form of passivity, where we are content to contemplate images of the world instead of living it, where mediated experience replaces direct experience.

alignments.french: Nous risquons alors de vivre par procuration, spectateurs d'un monde que nous regardons sans y être, connaissant tout en image et rien en réalité.
alignments.english: We then risk living vicariously, spectators of a world we watch without being in it, knowing everything in image and nothing in reality.

alignments.french: L'accessibilité, en rendant l'expérience réelle moins nécessaire en apparence, pourrait nous en détourner.
alignments.english: Accessibility, by making real experience seem less necessary, could divert us from it.

alignments.french: Il ne s'agit pas d'opposer l'expérience réelle noble à la représentation méprisable, ni de renoncer à l'accessibilité qui a tant apporté.
alignments.english: It is not about opposing noble real experience to contemptible representation, nor about renouncing the accessibility that has brought so much.

alignments.french: Il s'agit de ne pas confondre l'une avec l'autre, de garder conscience que voir n'est pas vivre, que l'image du monde n'est pas le monde.
alignments.english: It is about not confusing one with the other, maintaining awareness that seeing is not living, that the image of the world is not the world.

alignments.french: C'est préserver, à côté de l'accès facile aux représentations, le goût et la pratique de l'expérience réelle, de la présence, de l'engagement direct ; c'est se rappeler que certaines choses ne se connaissent qu'en les vivant, et que l'écran, si précieux soit-il pour donner accès, ne remplace pas ce contact avec le réel dont il ne transmet que l'apparence.
alignments.english: It is to preserve, alongside easy access to representations, the taste and practice of real experience, presence, and direct engagement; it is to remember that certain things can only be known by living them, and that the screen, however valuable for providing access, does not replace this contact with reality of which it only transmits the appearance.

alignments.french: Le monde à portée d'écran est un don ; le prendre pour le monde même serait s'enfermer dans sa représentation.
alignments.english: The world at our fingertips is a gift; taking it for the world itself would be to confine ourselves to its representation.

sentences: We often imagine that power rests on force: the one who commands does so because they can coerce, punish, or repress.
This view, while containing a grain of truth, is profoundly insufficient.

For no lasting power relies solely on force; all need, to maintain themselves, to be accepted, to appear legitimate, and to obtain not only the obedience of bodies but also the adherence, or at least the resignation, of minds.
And this legitimacy cannot be derived from force alone; it must be produced through a narrative, a myth, a story that justifies why it commands and why one should obey it.
Power needs narratives, and understanding this is to grasp one of the deepest mechanisms of societal life.
Let’s reflect on what makes a power obeyed.

Force alone is not enough, as no power has enough force to permanently coerce all those it governs; most must obey spontaneously, without being forced, because they consider obedience normal, legitimate, and self-evident.

However, this spontaneous obedience assumes that power is perceived as legitimate, that there is a narrative justifying its command: that it derives its authority from God, from birth, from the people, from competence, or from law.
This legitimizing narrative is what transforms force into authority, coercion into consented obedience; without it, power would be nothing but raw violence, precarious and constantly threatened.
These legitimizing narratives take various historical forms, but they all serve the same function.

The power that claims divine origin, the one that invokes blood and birth, the one that calls upon the will of the people, the one based on competence or law, all tell a story that justifies their command.
These narratives are not mere ornaments; they are constitutive of power, without which it would not be obeyed.
And they are all the more effective when they are believed, internalized, and taken for granted by those who obey.
The strongest power is not the one that coerces the most, but the one whose legitimacy narrative is most deeply internalized, to the point that obedience seems natural and dissent unthinkable.
This dependence of power on narratives has a double implication, one troubling and the other liberating.
Troubling: it reveals that power shapes minds, produces and disseminates the narratives that legitimize it, and acts on representations to be accepted.
Every power works to make people believe in its own legitimacy, to internalize in minds the narrative justifying obedience; it does not merely coerce bodies, it shapes consciences.
This action on representations, this manufacturing of consent, is one of the deepest and most insidious dimensions of power.
Liberating: because if power depends on narratives, and if these narratives are constructions, then they can be questioned, unmasked, and contested.
The power that seems most natural, most legitimate, most indisputable, rests on a narrative that could have been different, that is not necessary, and that can be interrogated.

Unmasking the narrative that legitimizes a power, showing that it is a construction and not an obvious truth, revealing the arbitrariness of what is presented as natural, is to shake the power at its very foundation.
All major challenges to power have begun with questioning the narrative that legitimized it, by refusing to accept as natural what was merely a construction.
Lucidity regarding the narratives of power is thus a weapon, the one that makes possible the contestation of what is presented as indisputable.
Understanding that power needs narratives is therefore to acquire an essential key to reading political life.
It is to learn to identify, behind every power, the narrative that legitimizes it, to question it, and not to take it for a natural given.

It is to understand that domination is not exercised solely through force, but through representations, and that the struggle for or against power is always also a struggle over narratives, over what is considered legitimate.

In a world where powers, both old and new, constantly produce the narratives that justify them, knowing how to unmask them, distinguishing real legitimacy from its fabrication, is a fundamental political skill — the one that distinguishes the aware citizen from the subject who obeys without knowing why.

sentences: Love claims to know the other like no one else does, to reach within them what others do not see, to understand them in their profound truth.
But it is also said that love is blind, that it idealizes the beloved, that it invents them according to its desire rather than seeing them as they are.
These two contradictory statements — love sees better, love is blind — express a deep paradox of love as a way of knowing others.
To love, is it to know the other better than anyone else, or to misunderstand them by adorning them with the colors of one's desire?
The question touches on what is most mysterious about love in its relationship to the truth of the beloved.
Let us first consider the thesis of blind love.
It is true that love idealizes, embellishes, and adorns the beloved with qualities they do not have or exaggerates.
The lover sees in the beloved a perfection that others do not see, attributes virtues to them, excuses their flaws, and contemplates them through the distorting prism of their desire.
This idealization is very real, and it explains the disappointments of love, when the veil is torn and the beloved appears as they are, different from the image one had of them.
In this sense, love misunderstands: it does not see the other as they are, but as desire dreams them; it invents an ideal being that is not the real being.
Love would then be the subtlest form of misunderstanding others, one that, under the guise of seeing them better, veils them behind an image.
And yet, the opposite thesis also has its truth.
For love, through the attention it gives to the beloved and the passionate interest it devotes to them, can reach in them what indifference does not see.

The one who loves observes the beloved with an intensity that no one else grants them, perceives their nuances, guesses their states, and opens up to their uniqueness with an acuity that only love provides.
In this sense, love sees better: it knows the beloved with a finer, more attentive, and deeper knowledge than the indifferent gaze.
It can perceive in the other possibilities, a beauty, a value that others do not see, not out of illusion, but through a sharper attention.
Love would then be the highest form of knowledge of others, one that, through passionate attention, reaches what indifference misses.
How can we reconcile these two truths?
Perhaps by distinguishing two forms or two moments of love.

There is a love that idealizes, that projects an image onto the other, that loves them less for what they are than for what we dream they might be; this love misrecognizes, and it is doomed to disillusion.

And there is a more mature love, which sees the other as they are, with their flaws and limitations, and loves them nonetheless, not despite their reality, but in their reality; this love knows, and it is stronger, for it has no illusions to lose.

The transition from one to the other — from the love that idealizes to the love that knows and loves the real — is perhaps the very maturation of love, what distinguishes illusory passion from true love.
There is more.
True love not only has the power to see the other as they are; it may also have the ability to help them become better, to reveal possibilities within them that they actualize under that gaze.
For being loved, being seen with that attention, that trust, that faith in what one can be, can help us to become it.
Love that sees the best in the other does not necessarily make mistakes; it can evoke what it perceives, calling the other to become what it sees in them.
In this sense, the idealization of love is not always an illusion; it can be a forward-looking vision that perceives possibilities and contributes to realizing them.
Love does not merely know the other; it participates in making them become.
Love is thus, in its relationship with others, both knowledge and misunderstanding, clarity and blindness, depending on its form and maturity.

Immature love idealizes and misunderstands; mature love sees and knows; and the highest love, perhaps, sees the other as they are while perceiving what they can become, knows their reality while believing in their possibilities.

To truly love is neither to blind oneself to the other nor to reduce them to what they are, but to know them in their truth while loving them enough to help them become the best version of themselves.

It is this conjunction of clarity and faith, of knowledge of the real and vision of the possible, that makes love neither a deceptive misunderstanding nor a cold knowledge, but the highest way to reach others: the one that sees them as they are and loves them as they could be.

sentences: The encounter with the stranger — from another people, another culture, another way of being — has always evoked mixed feelings: curiosity and fear, fascination and rejection, attraction and unease.
The stranger disturbs us because he is strange, because he embodies a way of being different from our own, which calls into question what we took for granted.
And yet, this encounter that disturbs us is also what reveals us, enriches us, and helps us grow.
Questioning our relationship with the stranger, with strangeness, is to understand both what we fear and what we gain in meeting the other.
What do we fear in the stranger?
His difference, first and foremost, which unsettles us.
The stranger embodies a way of being other than our own, which shows that our way is not the only one, that it is neither obvious nor necessary.
This revelation is unsettling: it shakes our certainties, relativizes our obviousness, deprives us of the comfort of believing that our way of life is the only natural one.
The stranger, by his mere existence, calls into question what we took for granted; and this questioning, while fruitful, is also unsettling.
We fear the stranger because he threatens our certainties, because he forces us to recognize the relativity of what we believed to be absolute.
We also fear the stranger as a threat, whether real or imaginary, to our identity, our security, our world.
This fear can have real foundations when the encounter is conflictual; but it is often exaggerated, fueled by imagination, projected onto the stranger who becomes the receptacle of our fears.
The stranger is easily transformed into a threat, a scapegoat, an embodiment of everything that worries us; their difference is perceived as a danger, their otherness as an aggression.
This fear of the stranger, when it is not controlled, leads to rejection, hostility, hatred, and the worst violence committed in the name of self-defense against the other.
But if the stranger disturbs us and frightens us, they are also what reveals and enriches us.
For their difference, which destabilizes our certainties, is also what makes us see them, relativizes them, and frees us from them.

By encountering another way of being, we discover that ours is just one way among many, and this discovery, while unsettling, is also liberating: it frees us from being trapped in a single vision, opens us to the diversity of ways of being human, and makes us broader.
The stranger is a mirror that reveals us to ourselves, showing us what is particular about us; they are a window onto other worlds, which expands our own.
What disturbs us in them is also what enriches us.
There is more.
Strangeness is not only found outside, in another people, another culture; it is also within us, closer than we think.
We are strangers to ourselves, as a thinker once said, carrying within us a part of shadow, the unknown, strangeness, that we do not control.

Recognizing the strangeness within oneself may be the condition for welcoming that of others: for the one who rejects all strangeness, who desires purity, an identity without mixture, the same without the other, that person rejects the stranger outside just as they repress the strangeness within.
Welcoming the other implies accepting one's own part of strangeness, renouncing the fantasy of a pure identity, and recognizing that we ourselves are traversed by otherness.
Our relationship with the stranger is thus revealing of who we are.

Fearing them, rejecting them, making them a scapegoat, is to yield to fear, to refuse the questioning they bring, to shut oneself in an identity that seeks to be pure; welcoming them, opening up to their difference, accepting to be destabilized, is to demonstrate a strength and generosity that enrich.

The encounter with the stranger is a test, which reveals whether we are capable of welcoming what disturbs us, allowing ourselves to be questioned, enriching ourselves with difference, or if we retreat into fear and rejection.

And for those who have learned a foreign language, entering a world different from their own, this test has already been faced and overcome: for learning the language of the stranger is already to welcome them, to open oneself to their world, to allow oneself to be enriched by their difference.
Learning a language may be the most beautiful response to the fear of the stranger: not the rejection of what disturbs us, but the welcoming of what enriches us.

sentences: Last night, the home team won an extraordinary match in the final seconds of the game.
The stadium had been full since early afternoon, and thousands of supporters had been waiting for this match for weeks.
The atmosphere was electric as soon as the players entered the field.
The start of the match was difficult for the home team.
The opponent scored a goal in the tenth minute, and the supporters remained silent for a long time.
The local players seemed nervous and struggled to control the ball during the first half of the match.
During the break, the coach spoke at length with his players in the locker room.
He reminded them of the importance of this match for the standings and asked them to stay calm and focused.
This speech clearly changed something, as the team returned to the field with much more energy.
When they returned from the locker room, the game completely changed.
The home players started to dominate the ball and create many scoring opportunities.
The young striker of the team, only nineteen years old, equalized the score with a powerful shot from outside the penalty area.
The stadium erupted with joy.
The match remained very tight until the last minutes.
Both teams had chances to score, but the goalkeepers made excellent saves.
Everyone thought the match would end in a draw, which would have been an honorable result for both teams.
But in stoppage time, in the ninety-third minute, the same young striker received a perfect cross and scored a beautiful header.
The stadium went wild.
The supporters cheered with joy for several minutes, and some even cried tears of happiness at this historic moment for the club.
After the match, the coach explained to the journalists that his players never gave up, even after conceding the first goal.
He also praised the young striker for his outstanding performance and announced that he would play an even more important role in the upcoming matches.
The next match will take place next Sunday, against one of the best teams in the league.
The supporters are already hoping to relive the same emotions and continue to celebrate this memorable victory in the streets of the city late into the night.
For the club, this victory is also important financially.
Winning this match allows them to stay at the top of the standings and hope for a place in European competition next season, which would bring a lot of money and visibility to the team.

sentences: My sister convinced me to try a yoga class with her.
I didn't really believe it.
"It's not real sports," I told her.
She laughed and replied, "Come see."
The class took place in a small quiet room, with soft music.
The teacher asked us to sit cross-legged.
I immediately felt pain in my legs!
For an hour, we did different poses.
Some were easy, others were almost impossible for me.
At the end of the class, the teacher asked us to lie down and close our eyes, without moving, for ten minutes.
I thought it would be easy.
In reality, it was very difficult to not think of anything!
After the class, I felt strangely calm and relaxed.
"So, still not real sports?" my sister asked me with a smile.
I had to admit that I was wrong.
I went back to the class the following week.

sentences: Every morning, I spend forty minutes in traffic to get to work.
Music makes this journey bearable.
I created a special playlist for the car, different from the one I listen to at home.
The first song is always the same: an energetic song to really wake me up.
Then come calmer songs, so I don't get annoyed in traffic.
Some mornings, when I'm late and stressed, I completely change the playlist to classical music.
It calms me down.
My colleague, who makes the same journey, asked me one day to send him my playlist.
He listened to it for a week, then he told me: 'It's too calm for me, I almost fell asleep!'
Everyone has their playlist, everyone has their journey.
But for me, these songs have become a real morning habit.
Without music, I think I would really hate this daily commute.

Nothing spectacular, no special effects.

There was a scene, towards the end, where the father said goodbye to his son.

sentences: Two years ago, we bought an old house to completely renovate.
Our friends had warned us: "Renovating an old house always takes more time and money than expected."
We didn't really believe them at first.
We thought we would finish the work in six months.
The first surprise came quickly: the house's electricity, installed in the sixties, needed to be completely redone.
Then we discovered moisture problems in the walls, which were invisible at the time of purchase.
Every month brought its share of new discoveries, often costly.
We had to revise our budget several times, saving on other projects.
Some evenings, tired from the dust and endless work, we doubted our decision.
But little by little, room by room, the house began to look like what we had imagined.
After two years of work, the house is finally almost finished.
Our friends were right about time and money.
But today, looking at this house that we transformed ourselves, we have no regrets.

sentences: We are constantly told that we need to reduce our sugar intake.
Doctors, magazines, and even advertisements for supposedly healthier products.
I know this recommendation by heart.
Yet, I still regularly give in to this craving for sugar, especially at the end of the day when fatigue sets in.
Experts explain that this craving is not just a matter of personal willpower.
Sugar activates pleasure-related circuits in our brain, somewhat like certain more problematic substances.
Moreover, sugar is now hidden in a huge number of products that you wouldn't suspect: sauces, industrial bread, and prepared meals marketed as balanced.
I have tried several times to drastically reduce my consumption.
The first few days are often the hardest, with noticeable irritability and fatigue.
Then, gradually, my cravings decrease, without completely disappearing.
A simple square of chocolate then satisfies me much more than before, when I used to eat a whole bar without really paying attention.
I have gotten into the habit of reading labels more carefully, discovering with surprise the amount of added sugar in products that didn't seem sweet to me at all.
This vigilance, tedious in the first few weeks, has become a reflex that has quietly changed my choices at the supermarket.
I don't think we should completely ban sugar, which seems almost impossible in our current diet.
But learning to measure it better, rather than consuming it automatically, changes a lot of things.

sentences: My dog, whom I adopted when he was still a puppy, taught me something I didn't expect to learn from an animal: patience.
I used to consider myself someone quite impatient, quickly annoyed by setbacks or unnecessary repetitions.
Training a puppy forced me to completely rethink this tendency.
In the first few weeks, I had to repeat the same commands over and over again, without immediate results.
My first reaction was often frustration.
I would get annoyed when he didn't understand what I was asking him, forgetting that a young dog learns at his own pace, without any intention of upsetting me.

A professional trainer, consulted after several difficult weeks, explained a simple yet enlightening thing to me: the owner's frustration always slows down the animal's learning, which feels this tension without understanding it.
This remark forced me to change my attitude, not only towards my dog but also in other areas of my life.
I started to apply, almost despite myself, this same patience with my colleagues, my loved ones, and myself.
This newly acquired patience now extends to situations where I would have never applied it before: an endless queue, a colleague slowly explaining something I already understood.
My dog, unknowingly, made me a bit more bearable for the people around me.
Today, my dog obeys much better, but I think I have changed more than he has during this learning process.
He has, without knowing it, taught me a lesson that I had never managed to learn in any other way.

sentences: The idea that video games can create a real addiction sparks a scientific and medical debate that is far from settled, despite the recent inclusion of this disorder in certain international medical classifications.

Supporters of recognizing this addiction rely on concerning clinical observations: some players do indeed develop compulsive behaviors, neglecting their sleep, social relationships, or professional obligations in favor of excessive gaming time, with real and documented consequences on their daily lives.

Critics of this classification highlight, on the contrary, a significant risk of methodological confusion: distinguishing between intense but chosen use, which is a source of legitimate pleasure, and a true compulsive pathology is a much more delicate task than some alarmist narratives in the media suggest.

These critics also remind us of an instructive historical precedent: similar moral panics have accompanied, in the past, the emergence of other entertainment mediums, from television to popular novels, which were often accused at the time of corrupting youth, without these fears always proving to be scientifically founded in the long term.

A consensus seems to be gradually emerging among researchers: while a minority of players do indeed develop problematic behaviors that warrant serious clinical attention, the hasty generalization of this reality to all video game players is likely an excessive simplification, driven more by generational cultural anxiety than by a rigorous and nuanced evaluation of the scientific data actually available on the issue.

sentences: This sentiment is worthy of the father of peoples, Mentor replied; it is to this kindness, and not to the vain magnificence of your city, that I recognize in you the heart of a true king.
But you must safeguard your honor, for the very interest of your kingdom.

Let me handle it; I will make these kings understand that you have committed to restoring Ulysses, if he is still alive, or at least his son, to royal power in Ithaca, and that you want to forcibly drive out all of Penelope's suitors.
They will have no trouble understanding that this war requires a large number of troops.
Thus, they will agree that you should only give them a small amount of support against the Daunians at first.
At these words, Idomeneus appeared like a man relieved of a heavy burden.
You save, dear friend, he said to Mentor, my honor, and the reputation of this emerging city, whose exhaustion you will conceal from all my neighbors.

But what appearance is there in saying that I want to send troops to Ithaca to restore Ulysses, or at least Telemachus, his son, while Telemachus himself is engaged in going to war against the Daunians!
Do not worry, Mentor replied; I will say nothing but the truth.

The ships you send to establish your trade will go to the coast of Epirus; they will do two things at once: one, to bring back foreign merchants to your coast, whom the excessive taxes had driven away from Salente; the other, to seek news of Ulysses.
If he is still alive, he must not be far from those seas that separate Greece from Italy; and it is said that he has been seen among the Phaeacians.

Penelope's suitors will be astonished to learn that he is ready to return with the help of a powerful ally.
The Ithacans will not dare to shake off the yoke.

sentences: Since his arrival in France with the invading army, Walter Schnaffs considered himself the most unfortunate of men.
He was overweight, walked with difficulty, breathed heavily, and suffered terribly from his very flat and very fat feet.

He was also peaceful and kind-hearted, by no means magnanimous or bloodthirsty, a father of four children whom he adored, and married to a young blonde woman, whose tenderness, little attentions, and kisses he desperately missed every evening.
He enjoyed getting up late and going to bed early, eating good food slowly, and drinking beer in the breweries.

He also thought that everything sweet in life disappears with death; and he harbored a dreadful hatred, both instinctive and reasoned, for cannons, rifles, revolvers, and sabers, but especially for bayonets, feeling incapable of maneuvering this swift weapon quickly enough to defend his large belly.

And when he lay down on the ground at night, rolled in his coat next to his snoring comrades, he thought longingly of his loved ones left behind and the dangers scattered along his path: -- If he were killed, what would happen to the little ones?
Who would feed and raise them?
At that very moment, they were not wealthy, despite the debts he had incurred in leaving them some money.
And Walter Schnaffs sometimes cried.
At the beginning of battles, he felt such weakness in his legs that he would have fallen, if he hadn't thought that the entire army would pass over his body.
The whistling of bullets made the hair on his skin stand on end.
For months he had been living like this in terror and anxiety.
His army corps was advancing towards Normandy; and one day he was sent on a reconnaissance mission with a small detachment that was simply meant to explore part of the countryside and then withdraw.
Everything seemed calm in the countryside; nothing indicated a prepared resistance.

Now, the Prussians were quietly descending into a small valley cut by deep ravines when a violent gunfire suddenly stopped them in their tracks, knocking down about twenty of their men; and a group of sharpshooters, suddenly emerging from a small wood no bigger than a hand, charged forward, bayonets fixed.

Stability: you cannot be forced to leave.

Conversely, renting offers real mobility, which is valuable in a job market where people often change jobs and cities.

sentences: Many people learned an instrument as children and then gave up.
Many adults dream of starting, but don't dare.
The question often comes up: is it worth it?
The benefits are real, but they need to be presented honestly, without exaggeration.
Learning an instrument develops coordination, memory, and the ability to maintain attention on a demanding task.

In children, some studies link musical practice to better language skills, although it's not always possible to establish a cause-and-effect relationship — children who do music often differ in other ways.
In adults, learning an instrument later in life is entirely possible, contrary to popular belief.
You may not achieve virtuosity, but you can find real enjoyment in playing.
It's also important to be honest about the difficulty.
An instrument requires regular practice, often daily, over many years.
The beginning is thankless: you produce unpleasant sounds, and progress is slow, often invisible at the moment.
This is precisely where the majority of people give up, not due to a lack of talent, but because of discouragement, usually within the first few months.
Those who persevere often mention the same key points.
A short but daily practice is better than a long weekly session.
Playing pieces that you love, even if simplified, maintains motivation better than dry exercises.
And accepting to be bad for a while is the condition for any progress.
The real benefit, in the end, may not be measurable.
It's the pleasure of making music yourself, rather than just consuming it.
Few people regret it.
Many regret having stopped.
