sentences: Philosophy suffers from a particular discredit, that of activities which produce nothing tangible.

It does not build bridges, heal diseases, or increase wealth; worse still, it does not even seem to progress, constantly returning to the same questions that the Ancients already asked, without ever resolving them.
In a world that judges everything by its usefulness and productivity, it appears as a relic, an intellectual luxury that is hard to define in terms of its purpose.
And yet, no civilization worthy of the name has done without it, and its apparent uselessness might well be a sign not of its vanity, but of its depth.
First, we must dispel a misunderstanding.
Philosophy is criticized for not resolving anything, as if it had failed to do what the sciences do.
But this criticism misunderstands its nature.

Philosophy does not deal with questions that observation or calculation could settle; it specifically addresses those that elude them, those concerning meaning, value, justice, goodness, and the nature of knowledge or consciousness.
These questions are not resolvable in the manner of a scientific problem, not because they are poorly posed, but because they engage who we are and what we hold to be important.
To criticize philosophy for not resolving them definitively is to reproach it for tackling what, by nature, cannot be concluded.
So what does it do, then, if it doesn't provide solutions?
It questions.
Its primary function is to challenge what is taken for granted, to uncover the assumptions that govern our lives without us ever having examined them.
We live on a mass of presuppositions — about what is right, about what is valuable, about what we ought to do — that we consider natural even though they are inherited, contingent, and debatable.
Philosophy has this uncomfortable virtue of making them visible, forcing us to justify them, and depriving us of the comfort of accepted ideas.
It doesn't give us answers; it enables us to ask the questions.
This function, which seems purely negative, is in reality a liberation.

For someone who has never questioned their presuppositions is not free: they endure them, thinking and acting according to frameworks they did not choose, believing they are making decisions when they are merely obeying invisible assumptions.
Becoming aware of these frameworks, examining them, is the beginning of freeing oneself, of thinking for oneself instead of thinking despite oneself.
In this sense, philosophy is not just additional knowledge, but an emancipation: it restores to the mind a freedom that habit and conformity had stolen from it.
Some will retort that this emancipation is a luxury, reserved for a few, with no effect on the course of the world.
That would underestimate the significance of ideas.
The concepts we have of justice, freedom, and human nature do not remain in books: they govern our institutions, our laws, and our ways of living together.
Major political transformations have almost always been preceded and nourished by a work of thought that first made conceivable what would become real.
Philosophy does not act directly, but it shapes the horizon in which action becomes possible; its apparent uselessness masks a slow and deep effectiveness.
However, its value is not reduced to its effects.

Philosophy responds to a need that is not for utility but for meaning: the distinctly human need to understand one's condition, to not go through existence without ever questioning what one does and why.
A life that would never ask these questions would not be less effective; it would be less fully human.
That is why philosophy, which serves no interest in the conventional sense, is indispensable in the sense that everything that makes life worth examining is.
Its uselessness is not a flaw; it is a sign that it touches on what, within us, goes beyond the mere need to live to question the very fact of living.

sentences: At forty, I had to relearn something I thought I had mastered since childhood: sleeping.
After years of degraded sleep, accumulated silently without me really paying attention, I finally decided to consult a specialist, tired of feeling constantly exhausted.

The specialist explained an idea that initially surprised me: sleep, contrary to what I thought, is not just a passive state that we endure, but a skill that can be cultivated, with specific habits to follow.

He proposed a structured program, called cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia, which involved completely reviewing my habits: a fixed bedtime and wake-up time, eliminating screens before sleeping, and reserving the bedroom solely for sleep.
The first few weeks were frustrating.
I felt like I was 'wasting time', lying down without sleeping, patiently waiting for my body to relearn a natural rhythm that had been lost for a long time.
Giving up certain evening habits — a late movie, reading in bed on my phone — required more willpower than I expected at first.
This sacrifice, modest in appearance, turned out to be much less difficult to maintain once I started to feel the first tangible benefits.
Gradually, however, the results appeared.
My ability to fall asleep became quicker, and my nighttime awakenings less frequent.

This experience taught me a broader lesson than just about sleep: some skills that we believe are permanently acquired can actually be lost over time, and sometimes deserve to be relearned, patiently, at any age in life.

sentences: From time to time, she would get up to fetch some bread, cider, and plates.
When she brought the coffee, she only set one cup down in front of him; then, filled with anger, he grumbled:
--Well, what about you?
--I don't want any, master.
--Why don't you want any?
--Because I don't like it.
Then he burst out again: "I don't like drinking my coffee alone, damn it...
If you don't want to start having some too, you can get lost, damn it...
Go get a cup, and make it quick."
She went to get a cup, sat back down, tasted the black liquid, grimaced, but under the furious gaze of her master, she swallowed it all.
Then he made her drink the first glass of the rinse, the second of the after-rinse, and the third of the kick-in-the-ass.
And Mr. Omont dismissed her.
"Go wash your dishes now, you're a good girl."
The same happened at dinner.
Then she had to play her game of dominoes; then he sent her to bed.
"Go to bed, I'll come up in a little while."
And she made her way to her room, an attic under the roof.
She said her prayers, undressed, and slipped into her sheets.
But suddenly she jumped up, startled.
A furious shout was shaking the house.
--Adélaïde?
She opened her door and answered from her attic:
"Here I am, master."
--Where are you?
--But I'm in my bed, so, my master.
Then he shouted, "Will you please come down, for God's sake...
I don't like sleeping alone, for God's sake..., and if you don't want to, you can get the hell out of here, for God's sake..."
Then she replied from upstairs, distraught, looking for her candle:
"--Here I am, my master!"

And he heard her little uncovered shoes tapping on the wooden stairs; and when she reached the last steps, he took her by the arm, and as soon as she left her narrow wooden shoes in front of the door next to the master's big clogs, he pushed her into his room grumbling:
"--Faster than that, then, for God's sake!"
And she kept repeating, not knowing what she was saying anymore:
"--Here I am, here I am, my master."

sentences: However, as if crossing the ice fields had been feasible, preparations for departure were actively continuing at the trading post.

Nothing should be overlooked for the safety of the expedition; everything had to be anticipated, taking into account not only the difficulties and fatigue but also the whims of this polar nature, which fiercely defends itself against human exploration.
The dog teams had received special care.
They were allowed to run around the fort so that the exercise would restore their somewhat stiffened strength from a long rest.
Overall, these animals were all in satisfactory condition and could, as long as they weren't overworked, undertake a long journey.
The sleds were carefully inspected.
The rough surface of the icefield would inevitably expose them to violent shocks.
Thus, they had to be reinforced in their main parts, their lower chassis, their curved front runners, etc.
This work rightfully belonged to the carpenter Mac Nap and his men, who made these vehicles as sturdy as possible.
In addition, two large sledges were built, one for transporting supplies and the other for transporting furs.
These sledges were to be pulled by domesticated reindeer, and they were perfectly suited for this purpose.
Furs were, as we can agree, a luxury cargo that it might not have been wise to burden oneself with.

But Jasper Hobson wanted, as much as possible, to safeguard the interests of the Hudson's Bay Company, being determined, moreover, to abandon these furs along the way if they compromised or hindered the caravan's progress.
There was no risk, moreover, since these precious furs, if left in the stores of the trading post, would inevitably be lost.
As for the provisions, that was another matter.
The supplies had to be abundant and easily transportable.
There was no way to rely on the products of the hunt.
The edible game, as soon as the passage was passable, would take the lead and would soon have gathered in the southern regions.

Therefore, preserved meats, corned beef, hare pâtés, dried fish, biscuits, whose supply was unfortunately quite limited, etc., a large reserve of sorrel and other delicacies, brandy, spirits for making hot drinks, etc., were placed in a special cart.
Jasper Hobson would have liked to take fuel, because for six hundred miles, he would find neither a tree, nor a shrub, nor moss, and one could not count on wreckage or driftwood from the sea.
But such an overload could not be allowed, and he had to give it up.
Fortunately, there would be no shortage of warm clothing; there would be plenty, comfortable, and if needed, they could draw fur from the cart.

sentences: Science has pushed the boundaries of our knowledge so far and solved so many puzzles once thought unsolvable that we are tempted to believe it will eventually explain everything, that there is no question it won't be able to answer one day.
However, this unlimited confidence in the power of science deserves to be questioned.

For it may be that there are questions to which science will never be able to respond, not due to temporary inadequacy, but because of a principled limit; things we will never know, not because we haven't found them yet, but because they inherently escape what we can know.
First, we must distinguish between two kinds of limits.
There are provisional limits, what we do not yet know but could know one day, the unresolved puzzles that progress might solve.

These limits are constantly receding, and the history of science is one of their continuous retreat; it would be unwise to preemptively set what science will never discover, given how it has disproven prophecies of its impotence.
But there may also be principled limits, questions that inherently escape scientific knowledge, not because we haven't found them yet, but because they do not fall within what science can establish.
It is these principled limits that we need to question.
A first category of such limits concerns, as we have seen, questions of value and meaning.
Science establishes what is, not what ought to be; it cannot resolve questions of purpose, value, or ultimate meaning, which do not pertain to the observation of facts.
These questions are not unresolved scientific puzzles that science will eventually clarify; they inherently escape its method, which deals with facts and not values.
That science progresses indefinitely will never bring it closer to answering the question of what is worth living for; this limit is not provisional, it is principled.

A second category perhaps concerns ultimate foundations, the first and last questions: why is there something rather than nothing? Where does the very existence of the universe and the laws that govern it come from?

Science can trace the chain of causes, explaining each thing by its antecedents, but it stumbles on this ultimate question of the very existence of everything, which it cannot resolve without presupposing what it is trying to explain.
Every scientific explanation presupposes something already given — laws, initial conditions — which it cannot account for without assuming it.

The question of the ultimate foundation, of the why of being itself, seems to escape by principle a science that always explains something by something else, and stumbles upon what has nothing before it.
A third limit, more troubling, perhaps concerns consciousness itself, that through which we know everything else.

Science can describe the processes that accompany consciousness, but it stumbles on the mystery of consciousness itself: how is it that there is lived experience, a subjective point of view, a 'what it feels like' to be conscious?

This mystery of subjectivity, the fact that there is someone who experiences, seems to resist a science that describes objects and processes, but struggles to account for the subjective experience itself.
Whether consciousness can ever fully explain itself, be completely grasped by science, is not assured; it may be that it involves a principled limit to self-knowledge.
Recognizing that there may be things we will never know does not belittle science, nor arbitrarily set limits to its power.
It is to acknowledge, with the clarity that extends science itself, that there could be principled limits to knowledge, questions that inherently escape what we can establish.

This recognition has value: it keeps us from the hubris that believes everything will one day be explained, that nothing will resist knowledge; it opens us to the possibility of mystery, of what exceeds knowledge; it restores a humility that the intoxication of scientific progress tends to make us lose.

Knowing that there may be things we will never know is not to give up knowing everything we can know; it is to recognize that human knowledge, however vast, may not be without limits — and that mystery, far from being only what we have not yet elucidated, could be a permanent dimension of our condition.

sentences: Jasper Hobson and a few of his companions therefore conducted this examination, searching carefully for any trace, any forgotten object, or even any footprint that could lead them on the right path.
But neither the ground nor the cooled ashes had kept any sufficient clues.
Some animal bones, scattered here and there, revealed nothing either.
The lieutenant, quite disheartened, was about to abandon this useless examination when he heard Mrs. Joliffe calling him from about a hundred paces to the left.
Jasper Hobson, Mrs. Paulina Barnett, the sergeant, the corporal, and a few others immediately headed towards the young Canadian woman, who remained still, attentively observing the ground.
When they arrived near her:
"Were you looking for traces?" Mrs. Joliffe said to Lieutenant Hobson.
"Well, here they are!"
And Mrs. Joliffe pointed out quite a number of footprints, very clearly preserved on a muddy ground.
This could be a characteristic clue, as the foot of an Indian and the foot of an Eskimo, as well as their footwear, differ completely.
But, above all, Jasper Hobson was struck by the peculiar arrangement of these footprints.
They indeed came from the pressure of a human foot, and even a shod foot, but, strangely, they seemed to have been made only with the sole of that foot.
The mark of the heel was missing.
Moreover, these footprints were remarkably numerous, close together, and crossed, although they were still contained within a very small circle.

sentences: Oh, how I pity you! replied Mentor: your passion is so fierce that you don't even feel it.
You think you are at peace, yet you are asking for death!
You dare to say that you are not defeated by love, yet you cannot tear yourself away from the nymph you love!
You see and hear only her; you are blind and deaf to everything else.
A man driven mad by fever says: I am not sick.

Oh blind Télémaque! you were ready to give up Penelope who is waiting for you, Ulysses whom you will see, Ithaca where you must reign, the glory and the high destiny that the gods have promised you through so many wonders they have performed in your favor: you were renouncing all these goods to live dishonored beside Eucharis!
Will you still say that love does not bind you to her?
What then troubles you? why do you want to die? why did you speak before the goddess with such passion?
I do not accuse you of bad faith; but I lament your blindness.
Flee, Télémaque, flee! one can only conquer Love by fleeing.
Against such an enemy, true courage consists of fearing and fleeing; but fleeing without deliberation, and without giving oneself the time to ever look back.
You have not forgotten the care you have cost me since your childhood, and the dangers from which you have emerged by my advice: either believe me, or suffer me to abandon you.
If you knew how painful it is for me to see you rushing towards your doom!
If you knew all that I have suffered while I dared not speak to you! the mother who gave you birth suffered less in the pains of childbirth.
I have been silent; I have swallowed my pain; I have stifled my sighs, to see if you would return to me.
Oh my son! my dear son! relieve my heart; give me back what is dearer to me than my own entrails; return to me Télémaque, whom I have lost; return to yourself.
If the wisdom in you overcomes love, I live, and I live happily; but if love drags you away despite wisdom, Mentor can no longer live.

sentences: And this is what has emboldened you, Maximilien; this is what makes my life both sweet and miserable, to the point that I often wonder which is better for me: the sorrow that my stepmother's harshness and her blind preference for her child once caused me, or the happiness filled with dangers that I experience when I see you.
Danger! Maximilien exclaimed; can you say such a harsh and unjust word?
Have you ever seen a more submissive slave than me?
You have allowed me to speak to you sometimes, Valentine, but you have forbidden me to follow you; I have obeyed.

Since I found a way to slip into this enclosure, to talk with you through this door, to be so close to you without seeing you, have I ever, tell me, asked to touch the hem of your dress through these bars?
Have I ever taken a step to cross this wall, a ridiculous obstacle for my youth and strength?
Never a reproach about your harshness, never a desire expressed out loud; I have been bound to my word like a knight of past times.
At least admit this, so that I do not think you unjust.
It's true, said Valentine, as she passed her slender finger between two boards, on which Maximilien placed his lips; it's true, you are an honest friend.
But still, you acted only out of self-interest, my dear Maximilien; you knew very well that from the day the slave became demanding, he would have to lose everything.

You promised me the friendship of a brother, to me who has no friends, to me whom my father forgets, to me whom my stepmother persecutes, and who has for consolation only the old man, motionless, mute, frozen, whose hand cannot grasp mine, whose eye alone can speak to me, and whose heart surely beats for me with a remnant of warmth.
Bitter mockery of fate that makes me an enemy and a victim of all those who are stronger than I, and gives me a corpse for support and for a friend!
Oh! truly, Maximilien, I repeat it to you, I am very unhappy, and you are right to love me for who I am and not for yourself.

sentences: Villefort flinched, Madame de Villefort let her son slide off her knees, and Valentine stood up, pale and silent like a statue.
Albert and Château-Renaud exchanged a second look that was even more astonished than the first.
The notary looked at Villefort.
--It's impossible, said the king's prosecutor; besides, Mr. d'Épinay cannot leave the drawing room at this moment.
--It is precisely at this moment, Barrois replied with the same firmness, that Mr. Noirtier, my master, wishes to discuss important matters with Mr. Franz d'Épinay.
--So he is speaking now, good old grandpa Noirtier? asked Édouard with his usual impertinence.
But this remark didn't even make Madame de Villefort smile, so preoccupied were their minds, and the situation seemed so solemn.
"Tell Mr. Noirtier, Villefort replied, that what he asks cannot be done.
--Then Mr. Noirtier informs these gentlemen, Barrois replied, that he will have himself brought to the drawing room.
The astonishment was at its peak.
A sort of smile appeared on Madame de Villefort's face.
Valentine, almost involuntarily, looked up at the ceiling to thank Heaven.
Valentine, said Mr. de Villefort, please go find out what this new fancy of your grandfather is.
Valentine quickly took a few steps to leave, but Mr. de Villefort changed his mind.
Wait, he said, I will accompany you.

--Excuse me, sir, said Franz in turn; it seems to me that since it is I whom Mr. Noirtier has requested, it is especially my duty to comply with his wishes; besides, I would be happy to present my respects to him, having not yet had the opportunity to seek this honor.
--Oh my God! said Villefort with visible concern, please do not trouble yourself.
--Excuse me, sir, said Franz in the tone of a man who has made up his mind.
I wish to not miss this opportunity to prove to Mr. Noirtier how wrong he would be to harbor any aversions against me that I am determined to overcome, whatever they may be, through my deep devotion.

And, without allowing himself to be held back any longer by Villefort, Franz stood up in turn and followed Valentine, who was already descending the stairs with the joy of a shipwrecked person who has found a rock.

sentences: The count approached, accompanied by Maximilien and Emmanuel: his calm and serene face stood in stark contrast to Albert's troubled expression, who was coming closer, followed by the four young men.
Three paces apart, Albert and the count stopped.

"Gentlemen," said Albert, "please come closer; I wish that not a word of what I am about to have the honor of saying to Mr. the Count of Monte-Cristo be lost; for what I am about to say to him must be repeated by you to anyone who wishes to hear it, no matter how strange my speech may seem to you.
--I am waiting, sir, said the count.

--Sir, said Albert, initially with a trembling voice, but gaining confidence as he spoke; sir, I reproached you for having revealed Mr. de Morcerf's conduct in Epirus; for, however guilty Mr. the Count de Morcerf may have been, I did not believe that it was you who had the right to punish him.
But today, sir, I know that this right has been granted to you.

It is not the betrayal of Fernand Mondego towards Ali-Pasha that makes me so quick to excuse you; it is the betrayal of the sinner Fernand towards you, it is the unheard-of misfortunes that resulted from this betrayal.
So I say it, so I proclaim it loudly: yes, sir, you were right to take revenge on my father, and I, his son, thank you for not having done more!"
The thunder, which fell among the spectators of this unexpected scene, would not have astonished them more than this declaration from Albert.

As for Monte-Cristo, his eyes had slowly turned to the sky with an expression of infinite gratitude, and he could not help but admire how Albert's fiery nature, of which he had known enough courage amidst the Roman bandits, had suddenly yielded to this sudden humiliation.
Thus he recognized the influence of Mercédès, and understood how this noble heart had not opposed the sacrifice that she knew in advance would be in vain.
Now, sir, Albert said, if you find that the apologies I just made to you are sufficient, your hand, please.
After the rare merit of infallibility that seems to be yours, the first of all merits, in my opinion, is knowing how to admit one's faults.
But this admission concerns me alone.
I acted rightly according to men, but you, you acted rightly according to God.
Only an angel could save one of us from death, and the angel descended from heaven, if not to make us two friends, alas! fate makes that impossible, but at least two men who respect each other.

sentences: I run three times a week, early in the morning, at six o'clock.
My friends tell me, 'You are crazy!'
Maybe.
But I love it.
It wasn't easy at first.
The first week, everything was difficult.
Outside, it was cold and dark.
I was tired and my legs hurt.
But I kept going.
Now, I run for thirty minutes without stopping.
I'm not fast, but I run.
In the morning, the city is calm.
There are few cars.
The air is fresh.
I run in the park, near the lake.
The ducks are still sleeping.
There are other morning runners.
We don't know each other's names, but we know each other.
The lady in the yellow t-shirt.
The man with his dog.
We wave to each other.
After the run, I take a hot shower and a nice breakfast.
At work, my colleagues arrive tired.
As for me, I am in shape.
Morning exercise is my secret.
For my thirty-fourth birthday, I treated myself to a surprising gift: a skateboard.
My friends laughed.
"A skateboard?
At your age?"
When I was a teenager, I dreamed of doing it, but I never dared.
This year, it's now or never.
On the first day, at the park, I was very nervous.
I put one foot on the board.
It moved.
I put my other foot on, and I fell, like a sack of potatoes.
For two weeks, it was difficult.
I fell every day and had bruises.
Several times, I thought about quitting.
And then I met Théo, who is ten years old and skates like a champion.
One day, he came over and said, 'Sir, you are looking at your feet.
You need to look far ahead.
And bend your knees, or you'll fall.'
Théo's advice changed everything.
Every Saturday, my little teacher gave me a new lesson.
In exchange, I bought him an orange juice.
Last month, the big moment arrived: I crossed the whole park without falling, with the wind on my face.
Théo applauded.
I was as proud as a child.
I will never be a champion.
I still fall, but every Saturday, I make a little progress.
There is no age to learn.
There are just knees to bend and a bit of courage to find.

sentences: When I told my mother that I was moving in with roommates at thirty-two, she fell silent with worry on the phone.
But come on... you had your own apartment!
For her generation, living with others after finishing studies feels like a step backward, almost like a failure.
However, more and more adults are making this choice, often without regret.
The first reason is obviously economic.
In big cities, rents have become crazy.
My twenty-five square meter studio cost me almost half of my salary.
Today, I pay a third less for a room in a large, bright apartment, with a living room where you can really invite friends, a proper kitchen, and even a balcony.
With the same budget, living with roommates offers a quality of life that a studio can never provide.
But reducing shared living to just a matter of money would be a mistake.
What surprised me the most in my old studio was the evening silence.
It's not said enough: living alone can be heavy.
Coming home and telling someone about your day, sharing an impromptu meal, watching a movie with three people on a Tuesday night — these little things change the tone of a week.
Of course, not everything is idyllic.
You have to deal with the habits of others: the dirty dishes left out, the loud music, surprise guests.
We learned to talk about it before tensions rose, and we established a few simple rules.
Shared living is a school of compromise, and at thirty, you experience it better than at twenty: you know your limits, you dare to express them, and you more easily respect those of others.
Finally, there are the nice surprises.
Léa, my roommate, has become a close friend.
Simon introduced me to climbing.
Our Sunday night dinners have become an institution that no one wants to miss.
My mother finally came over for lunch.
As she was leaving, she whispered to me, "It's true that this apartment is nice.
And your roommates are nice too."
Coming from her, it's a total victory.
Living with roommates at thirty isn't a step backward.
Sometimes, it's simply a smarter — and warmer — way to live in the city.

sentences: It was better before.
The phrase is so widespread that it seems obvious.
Before, people were more polite, food had more flavor, summers were more beautiful, and life was simpler.
Each of us, at some point, has thought or said it.
This feeling, nostalgia, is universal and often sweet.
Yet it deserves to be examined, because it is largely based on an illusion — an illusion created by the very functioning of our memory.
Our memory, in fact, is not an impartial historian: it is a painter that embellishes.
It preferentially retains happy moments and allows difficulties, troubles, and the little miseries of everyday life from the past to fade away.
When we talk about our childhood, we summon sunny summers, laughter, vacations — not the hours of boredom, arguments, or forgotten anxieties.
The past appears better to us not because it was, but because we only keep the best of it.
The 'good old days' is a work of art, composed by forgetfulness.
This illusion is compounded by a bias of comparison.
We compare a past that has been cleansed of its discomforts to a present that we experience in all its fullness — with its concrete worries, immediate irritations, and uncertainty.
The playing field is not level.
The present always has the disadvantage of being real, while the past has the charm of what is complete and neatly arranged.
It's no surprise, then, that it prevails.
Should we, then, condemn nostalgia as a mere mistake?
That would be going too far.
Psychologists who study it recognize its virtues.
Remembering fondly the loved ones, the places of one's childhood, the music of an era warms the heart and gives the feeling of continuity of self through time.
Nostalgia connects: it ties us to those who are no longer here, to what we have been.
Well-lived, it is a form of gratitude towards one's own history.
The trap is not to feel nostalgia, but to let oneself be trapped in it.
For there is a sterile, even dangerous nostalgia.
In the scale of a life, it leads to living turned backward, always finding the present mediocre and the future threatening, and missing out on the good that the moment offers.
On a societal level, the illusion of a lost golden age fuels speeches that promise to 'return' to an idealized past that never existed.
Collective nostalgia, when it becomes political, can come at a very high cost.
Wisdom lies, as often, in moderation and discernment.
To savor happy memories without forgetting that they are embellished.
To draw from the past sweetness and strength, not a judgment against the present.
To remember that our own 'good old days' were, at the time, an anxious and imperfect present — just like today.
And to finally remember this: in a few years, this present that we judge so dull may, in turn, become the 'good old days' that we will regret.
As much as possible, while it is here, let's try to inhabit it.

sentences: For my niece Chloé's birthday, I wanted to make a chocolate cake myself.
It was a bad idea.
I had found a recipe on the internet.
In the photo, the cake was beautiful.
I started at two o'clock.
I broke the eggs, melted the chocolate, added the flour and the sugar.
Everything was going well.
But I didn't have a scale.
So I guessed the quantities.
"Two hundred grams of flour?
That should be about this much."
First mistake.
I put the cake in the oven.
The recipe said thirty minutes at one hundred eighty degrees.
But my oven is old and it heats too much.
Second mistake: I didn't watch it.
I was replying to messages.
After twenty-five minutes, I felt something.
I opened the oven: the cake was black on the edges and completely flat in the middle.
It didn't look like the photo at all.
I felt like crying, then like laughing.
I cut off the black edges and put sugar on top to hide the rest.
When Chloé arrived, she looked at the cake.
She is seven years old, so she is honest.
Your cake is strange.
I know.
She took some candies out of her pocket and put them on top.
There you go!
Now it looks nice.
We ate it.
And it was good.

sentences: In English, there is only one word: 'you.'
In French, you have to choose between 'tu' and 'vous.'
For my English friend Tom, it's one of the most difficult things.
The general rule seems simple.
You say 'tu' to family, friends, and close colleagues.
You say 'vous' to strangers and in official situations.
But in real life, it's much more complicated.
Tom told me about several mistakes.
One day, he addressed a sixty-year-old man informally in a store.
The man seemed surprised and cold.
In France, addressing an older stranger informally can seem rude.
Another time, it was the opposite.
He used the formal 'vous' with a friend of his age for two hours.
In the end, the other one said to him, laughing: 'We can use the informal 'tu', you know!'
The rules also change depending on the environment.
In some companies, everyone uses 'tu', even the director.
In others, you use 'vous' with your boss for twenty years.
I gave Tom a simple piece of advice: when you don't know, start with 'vous'.
There is a magic phrase: 'Can we use 'tu'?'
It is often the oldest person who suggests it.
Tom learned it by heart.

sentences: According to estimates, a person living in a city is exposed to several thousand advertising messages each day.
Billboards, screens, apps, videos, brand names on clothing: advertising takes up a significant part of our visual environment.
Most people claim to be insensitive to it.
"Advertising doesn't work on me."
It's precisely this belief that makes it effective.
Because modern advertising doesn't just aim to promote a product.
It often targets something more subtle: associating a brand with an emotion, a status, an identity.
We're not selling a car, but freedom; not a drink, but friendship.
This mechanism works outside of conscious decision-making.
We don't need to believe the advertisement for it to work: it just needs to create an association in our memory.
When it comes time to choose, a brand comes to mind more easily, without us knowing why.
Repetition plays a central role.
A message seen once is forgotten; seen a thousand times, it becomes familiar, and the brain often confuses familiarity with trust.
Recognizing this does not make one immune — these mechanisms still operate even when we are aware of them.
But a few reflexes can reduce their influence.
Asking oneself, in front of a sudden desire, where it comes from.
Waiting before a purchase, until the effect wears off.
Using tools that limit online advertising.
And being wary of content that pretends not to be advertising: influencer recommendations, promotional articles.
Advertising is neither a conspiracy nor a disaster.
It is an environment, and like any environment, it shapes us.
The minimum is to know that it is there.

sentences: We have seen that "free" services come at the cost of our attention.
They also come at the cost of something else, something even more intimate: our personal data.
Every search, every purchase, every movement, every message leaves a trace, and these traces, when gathered, create a portrait of unsettling precision.
This portrait has value, and it is partly what we give up in exchange for free services.
For a long time, this concern was brushed aside with the phrase: "I have nothing to hide."
The argument seems reasonable; however, it is fragile.
The protection of privacy has never been about hiding faults, but about maintaining a space that belongs only to oneself.
Closing the door to one's room is not an admission of a guilty secret; it is an exercise of basic freedom.
Yet it is precisely this door that the massive collection of data tends to keep open at all times.
Moreover, the objection of "nothing to hide" assumes that this data will never be used against us.
Nothing guarantees that.
A seemingly harmless piece of information today can become compromising tomorrow if laws change or if power changes hands.
Data collected for a specific purpose can be redirected for another.
Entrusting your traces is like betting on the future, a bet whose terms we cannot control.
We must also move beyond just the individual perspective.

Even if everyone willingly accepted this exchange for their own sake, the accumulation of our data gives a few companies considerable power: the power to predict our behaviors, to shape our choices, and sometimes to influence our opinions.
This power does not only concern the individuals who have, apparently, consented; it weighs on society as a whole.
Defending privacy is therefore not a whim of people who have something to hide.
It is defending a condition of freedom, for oneself and for others.
The free services offered to us come at a price, and this price is not only personal: it is, ultimately, political.

sentences: To misname an object is to add to the misfortune of this world.

This statement from a writer, surprisingly grave for someone who sees language as merely a tool, expresses what could be called an ethics of language: the idea that the way we name things is not morally neutral, that the precision, accuracy, and honesty of language are demands that are not only intellectual but also ethical.
At the end of these reflections on the powers of language, this idea deserves to be contemplated, as it brings together and crowns all that has come before.
Why would misnaming add to the misfortune of the world?
Because, as we have seen, language is not a neutral mirror of reality, but a force that shapes it.
To name is to interpret, to guide perception, to shape judgment; the words we use to designate things do not merely describe them, they partially constitute them for us.

Thus, misnaming — using false, vague, misleading words that distort what they refer to — is not just a simple blunder; it distorts our relationship to reality, muddles our understanding, and misleads the judgment of those we are speaking to.
The inaccurate word spreads error, the euphemism masks reality, and the loaded word stirs passion where clarity is needed.
In this sense, misnaming harms, spreads confusion, and adds its grain of falsehood to the disorder of the world.
This ethic of language first demands precision.

Searching for the right word, the one that expresses exactly what we mean, neither more nor less, is not a stylist's whim; it is a requirement of truth, a respect for reality and for the person we are speaking to.
The approximate word, the roughly right term, the vague expression that covers different realities, fosters confusion in thought; the precision of language is the condition for clarity of mind.
Those who strive to name things correctly also strive, simultaneously, to think correctly, because thought and its expression are inseparable.
The quest for the right word is a quest for truth.
This ethic also demands honesty.
It is not enough to name things precisely; one must also not use the power of words to deceive, manipulate, or conceal.

The euphemism that softens the unacceptable, the loaded word that prejudges, the phrase that manipulates emotions, are abuses of language, ways of 'misnaming' that, under the guise of speech, distort the relationship to reality and to others.
The honesty of language consists in not exploiting its power against the truth, in not using words to hide what they should reveal.
It is the refusal of lies that are not only explicit but also insidious, those that slip into the very choice of words.
This ethic ultimately demands a form of justice.
For to name things well is also to give things and beings their rightful name, to reject words that belittle, exclude, and dehumanize, as well as words that flatter and deceive.

The way we name human beings, in particular, is never neutral: the word that reduces a person to a category, that confines them to a label, that designates them for exclusion, inflicts violence; the word that recognizes them in their dignity delivers justice.
There is a justice in language, which consists of naming each person and each thing according to what they are, without belittling or distorting them.
To misname beings is to do them wrong; to name them well is to give them what they are owed.
Thus, the ethic of language crowns our reflection on its powers.
If language shapes our world, guides our thought, reveals or conceals experience, and constitutes our relationship to reality and to others, then the way we use it entails a responsibility.
To name things well is not a secondary elegance, but a duty: of truth, towards reality; of honesty, towards others; of justice, towards beings.

And for those who are learning a language, this requirement takes on a particular meaning: for learning to name well, in a new language as well as in one's own, to seek the right word, to avoid the wrong word, is not just to gain mastery; it is to learn a more truthful, more honest, more just relationship to the world and to others.
The care of language is the care of truth — and perhaps this is where mastery of a language meets wisdom.

At this point, sleep began to overtake Alice.
She kept repeating, half asleep: "Do cats eat bats?
Do cats eat bats?"
And sometimes: "Do bats eat cats?"
Because you see, since she couldn't answer either of these questions, it didn't matter how she asked them.
She was dozing off and began to dream that she was walking along holding Dinah by the hand, very seriously saying to her: "Come on, Dinah, tell me the truth, have you ever eaten bats?"
When suddenly, poof! there she was lying on a pile of sticks and dry leaves, -- and she had finished falling.

Quickly, she gets back on her feet and looks up; but everything is dark up there.

She was only two steps away: but as he turned the corner, the Rabbit had vanished.
She then found herself in a long, low room, lit by a row of lamps hanging from the ceiling.
